atoms.b:
The term “generation” refers to a ((++group)) of people who are born within a certain time period and share similar ((++historical)) experiences.
However, it is important to ((++distinguish)) between ((++generational)) patterns and individual reality.

Applying generalised characteristics to all members of a generation is a form of ((++stereotypical_thinking)) and must be avoided.
((++Individual_traits)) can vary significantly within each ((++generation)) based on family background, location, and other personal circumstances.

Baby Boomers grew up during an ((economic)) boom in the 1950s–60s, the Civil Rights Movement, and the Vietnam War. Some Baby Boomers later pioneered computing and internet ((technology)), while others became ((environmental)) activists who fought for changes and established Earth Day in 1970.

atoms.b: Generation X grew up during the rise of the early ((internet)), making them a “bridge generation” between analogue and digital ((technology)). Generation X experienced multiple economic recessions and witnessed corporate downsizing and lay-offs, which shaped their ((scepticism)) about company loyalty.

Millennials grew up during the rise of personal ((computers)). They faced unique economic challenges, such as the 2008 recession and ((soaring_costs)) regarding housing. Many Millennials prioritise meaningful work and ((work-life-balance)).

Generation Z is the first true “digital native” generation, growing up entirely with smartphones, ((social_media)), and the internet as normal parts of life. Generation Z came of age with ((climate_change_awareness)) as a standard part of education.

Generation Alpha is the first generation born entirely in the ((21st_century)), growing up with artificial intelligence, smartphones, social media, and ((global_connectivity)) as normal. Their education has been shaped by COVID-19 pandemic disruptions, ((remote_learning)), and increasing integration of technology in schools.
